newsitem.title: GERMANY: Focus-Bonn grapples budget deficits to make EMU.
newsitem.headline: Focus-Bonn grapples budget deficits to make EMU.

text.p: Germany, struggling to qualify for Europe's single currency, prepared on Wednesday to tackle its growing budget deficit with more public borrowing and sales of some of its shares in telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom AG.

Government coalition sources said 1997 tax revenues would be nearly 20 billion marks ($12 billion) less than expected, opening up a gaping budget hole and casting doubts about Bonn's ability to join the economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, trying to soften the blow of the tax revenue news to be announced officially on Thursday, said he was sure Germany could still qualify for the euro.

But Bonn had to take bold steps, such as higher new borrowing or selling part of its stake in Deutsche Telekom, he indicated. An emergency savings package could be announced as early as Thursday evening, Bonn officials said.

Economists said Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government had to clamp down hard if it wanted EMU to start on time and in line with the stringent Maastricht criteria. Germany has pushed hard to keep other EU states from weakening the criteria for EMU.
"Germany really has to make its mind up pretty quickly what kind of EMU it wants," Darren Williams at UBS in London said.
"If it doesn't do something about this shortfall, it's going to be incredibly difficult for it to be choosy about its EMU partners."

A Reuters survey of 35 European economists published on Wednesday showed Germany was the only country failing to make progress on achieving the Maastricht targets. But another poll showed economists expected Germany to be in the first EMU wave.
In a foretaste of what could come in Bonn, the state of Hesse -- where the banking capital Frankfurt is located -- said it was planning a budget freeze in light of the tax shortfall.

Squabbling about politically sensitive measures also started in Bonn, with Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners adamantly ruling out tax hikes and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe declaring his budget could be cut no more.

The bad news about the tax shortfall leaked as federal, state and central bank officials met private-sector advisers in the eastern town of Schwerin to compile tax revenue estimates. They will formally deliver the new tax estimate on Thursday.
"We will do everything we can to fulfil the Maastricht criteria and we will fulfil them," Waigel told reporters. "We are prepared with a number of corresponding measures."
New borrowing beyond the 53.4 billion marks ($31 billion) planned in the 1997 budget "cannot be ruled out", he added.
Waigel said Bonn was also considering selling part of its 74 percent stake in Deutsche Telekom AG earlier than the originally planned date of 2000.
His comments sent a shiver through the Frankfurt bourse, knocking the 30-share DAX index down 21.46 points to 3,573.69. Telekom shares fell 2.3 percent to 39.20 marks.

Government officials said Waigel could also save more by slashing retraining programmes run by the Federal Labour Office, whose spending has mushroomed because of Germany's record unemployment of about 4.1 million this year.
Bonn could also collect more tax revenues by taxing hidden revenues the power utility companies have put aside to pay for mothballing nuclear power plants, they said.

Germany could borrow more than planned this year and still meet the Maastricht deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product, government officials say, because the planned overall deficit this year amounts to only 2.5 percent of GDP.
Germany's overall 1997 public borrowing, including that of its federal states, is due to reach 99.5 billion marks. Federal borrowing accounts for 53.3 billion of that figure.
FDP chairman Wolfgang Gerhardt said tax increases would be "poison for the economy" and said just about any other way to increase revenue would be better.
The stability of the euro would not be significantly undermined if Germany's budget deficit slighly exceeded the Maastricht targets, he told Stern magazine.
